text.p: Den norske Bank ASA, Norway's top commercial bank, said Wednesday that cost cuts and a healthy national economy helped lift its 1996 net profits by 1.7 percent.
Earnings rose to 2.70 billion crowns ($408.9 million) from 2.66 billion ($403 million) in 1995, corresponding to earnings per share of 4.22 crowns and a 20 percent return on equity, DnB said.

"The strong results reflect sound operations, reduced costs and a healthy trend in the Norwegian economy," group managing director Finn Hvistendahl said in a statement. "This has coincided with a favourable loan-loss trend and continued reversals on previous loan losses."

The volume of new loan losses was 837 million crowns ($127 million) in 1996, down from 1.25 billion ($189 million) in the previous year. Net reversals -- or writebacks on bad loans turned good -- fell to 380 million crowns ($58 million) from 479 million ($73 million).
DnB is 52-percent owned by the Norwegian government, which bailed out major banks of a financial crisis in the early 1990s.
Analysts said that a fight DnB has with tax authorities over tax losses carried forward from the crisis years was putting a questionmark over the bank's future net earnings.

"When they start paying taxes and normal provisions I have them earning three crowns per share, which would mean a sustainable level of 1.5 crowns in dividend," said bank analyst James Alexander of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London.

The 1996 accounts include a tax charge of 22 million crowns ($3.3 million), up from six million ($908,680) in 1995. If the taxman had his way, DnB would have paid 617 million crowns ($93.4 million) in taxes in 1996, the bank said.
"DnB has a complicated tax situation," said Alexander. "It probably won't start paying normal taxes until in 1998."
